title: Even the wise drift (1 Kings 11:1–13)
hookLine: Solomon's heart turns in old age
carry: one small choice at a time

cards: A heart that hears. That's what Solomon asked for in a dream, at the very start.
Since then he has judged between two mothers, built a house in quiet, prayed, saying heaven itself can't hold God, and asked that strangers be heard. A queen came to test him and went home amazed.
Then the text turns a page and writes a sentence that begins, when Solomon was old. There's no single scene of falling. It's slower than that.

teach.b: The text says Solomon loved many foreign women, and gives the number itself: seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines.
The Torah had warned that a king must not multiply wives, so that his heart not turn away.
And verse four says just that, in the 1917 Jewish translation: "when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods."

He built high places for the gods of his wives' peoples, on the hill before Jerusalem. But the text doesn't let this be anyone else's fault. The LORD is angry with Solomon, because his heart was turned.
His heart, the verse goes on, was not whole, in Hebrew not shalem, with God, as David's heart had been. The Talmud tells that Solomon reasoned he could take many wives and not be turned, and he was.
His story opens with a heart, lev shomea, a listening heart. It closes with a heart that turned. Same heart.
And there's no single moment of turning: the text lists marriages, then shrines for the gods of his wives, one after another. Nobody in the story wakes up one morning a different person.
Many readers take Solomon's drift as a warning.
The story doesn't call wisdom worthless; it shows that wisdom alone didn't keep him from turning. A king given wisdom in a dream still needed to keep choosing, every year, into old age.
And the cost comes due in the next generation.

how: Jews read Solomon's later years in the book of Kings, and the Talmud uses his story to show why the Torah's limits on a king matter even for the wise.

o: whole: a heart undivided, all there
wise: able to answer any riddle at all
peace: an end to every war and quarrel

games.q: you're a king known for wisdom. the Torah warns kings against many wives, lest the heart turn. what do you tell yourself?
o: the warning is for kings less wise than me.
keep the limit, because even wisdom can drift.
ask a prophet to decide for you.
games.why: the Talmud tells that Solomon reasoned he could take many wives and not be turned, and the text says that when he was old, his heart was turned.

practice: Is there something that matters to you that has slowly slipped, a habit of prayer, a friendship you used to tend, a value you once held tightly?
With no scolding, trace it back to the small choice where the drift started, then name one small choice that could turn you back toward it. If you pray, you can ask for a whole heart.

wordCard.voice: Shalem. The Hebrew word for whole, the wholeness Solomon's heart lost toward God as he grew old. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: whole, complete. Solomon's heart was not shalem with God.

carryVoice: Your line: one small choice at a time. The week in lines: a listening heart, the real mother gives way, finished before anyone hears it, a place to turn toward, hear the stranger too, the half was not told, and this one. Day seven hundred sixty-three.
